doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Medical training in Cleveland and joining a neurosurgical team in the Army
summary: Budd chose Cleveland for surgery, baseball and jazz, then served in the Army learning neurosurgery.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: What was your specialty in medicine — and is your specialty?

Well everything. I was a general practitioner, which included — and I went away to Cleveland, Ohio to get training in surgery. And one of the doctors in Cleveland was a successful surgeon and had trained at Charity Hospital in Cleveland. And he suggested that that would be a great place to go that it had a wonderful program, and also had a major league baseball team of course, and also at that time all kinds of jazz musicians © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

were there. And I couldn’t go wrong, so I said I’ll go there and take a year there at least, and I stayed the second year and I stayed the third year and then I decided I was going to stay there and practice there. So I would practice surgery, plus I had one month of obstetrical training besides, and so you did surgery fairly good, and obstetrics, and general medicine, until the war came along and then I went in the Army. I was still a Canadian but I went over in the American Army and was attached for a while to a place doing nothing, in Madison, Wisconsin, as a house doctor or something. Most of the patients were guys with flat feet or backaches or hangovers, things like that. They were fellows who were in the Air Force but had wanted to be pilots but were flushed out and wound up radio operators and radio mechanics, good jobs but they were frustrated. They were my patients. And then when they were preparing for the invasion in Normandy, they picked about four guys who were up there doing little or nothing and sent us down to join a group, the Fourth Auxiliary Surgical Group, which that became later, for the next war, the Mobile Auxiliary Surgical Hospital which is MASH. But we were the fourth Auxiliary Surgical Group. There were five of them and they were all made up of teams and the chief, the Colonel, said “what did you do in practice?” And I said “most everything, surgery and medicine.” He said “did you do any neurosurgery?” And I said “no.” He said “would you like to learn?” I said “yes, I would.” So he said “there’s a chief of a neurosurgical team that needs an assistant and maybe you could go with him.” So I went with him and he was bound to teach me and he taught me more in two years with him than I had learned in four years of medical school, how to do things. We did nothing but brain and spine injuries, twelve hours a day for two years. And you get to know how to do more than many people in civilian practice would ever see that many brain injuries we did. What I might have done after that was go back to medical school and learn about the rest of neurosurgery like tumors and stuff like that, but I decided I’d been away from my children for two years and my wife and I’ll do it next year and I’ll do it next year, and it faded away.
